question: Are the rounding-tie compressions between capabilities whose movement signatures are nearly identical (benign aliases of one another) or between dissimilar capabilities (real information loss)?
why: The closed tie-risk study measured that ties happen and how close the raw scores are. It did not measure whether the tied capabilities are near-duplicates in movement, which changes how a consumer should read a sub-1-percent compression.

method.signature_token: one token per movement entry, decoded from the stored JSON signature string, e.g. ["L",-3,3] or ["R",-1,2,-1]
method.similarity: Jaccard index |A intersect B| / |A union B| over the token sets of the two tied types
method.tied_set: the 31 distinct-score tied pairs (raw scores differ, exact gap < 1, stored board equal)
method.reference_set: every distinct-capability pair in the same nine cells (same extraction as the closed gap analysis)
method.aggregation: per-size and pooled; report median, quartiles and the reference percentile of the tied median

pre_written_decision.benign_concentration: tied-pair median Jaccard is at or above the 90th percentile of the reference set
pre_written_decision.dissimilar_ties: tied-pair median Jaccard is at or below the 75th percentile of the reference set

endpoint: one of benign_concentration | dissimilar_ties | inconclusive_similarity, plus the two distributions
cost_estimate: under 1 minute of compute, one read of the stored 3.3 MB result; no rule generation
consumer: the tie-risk report and any backend consumer choosing whether a sub-1-percent integer compression is acceptable; a benign result would justify tolerating ties, a dissimilar result would not
limits: 22 unordered signature classes among 31 tied pairs, so the tied distribution is small
syntactic movement similarity is not strategic equivalence
no strength, utility or human-price claim
nonclaims: not a rerun of the closed tie-risk scan
not a solver or game-strength experiment
